content: If bleeding persists or occurs after previously regular menstrual cycles, it is important to investigate potential causes such as pregnancy or malignancy. If both pathology and pregnancy are ruled out, irregular bleeding may resolve over time or with a change to a different contraceptive product. Women undergoing contraceptive therapy may experience amenorrhea (absence of withdrawal bleeding), even if they are not pregnant. If scheduled withdrawal bleeding does not occur, pregnancy should be considered, especially if the patient has not adhered to the prescribed dosing schedule (e.g., missed one or more active tablets or started taking them later than recommended). If the patient has adhered to the prescribed regimen but misses two consecutive periods, pregnancy must be ruled out. Contraceptive use is not necessary during pregnancy, and the medication should be discontinued if pregnancy is confirmed. Extensive studies have demonstrated no increased risk of birth defects in women who used oral contraceptives prior to pregnancy. Additionally, there is no evidence of teratogenic effects, particularly concerning cardiac anomalies and limb-reduction defects, when oral contraceptives are inadvertently taken during early pregnancy. Oral contraceptives should not be used to induce withdrawal bleeding as a test for pregnancy, nor should they be used during pregnancy to treat threatened or habitual abortion. For any patient who has missed two consecutive periods, pregnancy should be ruled out before continuing oral contraceptive use. If the patient has not adhered to the prescribed schedule, pregnancy should be considered at the time of the first missed period. Oral contraceptive use should be discontinued if pregnancy is confirmed. Contraceptive hormones and their metabolites are present in human breast milk. Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) can reduce milk production in breastfeeding women, and this reduction can occur at any time but is less likely once breastfeeding is well-established. When possible, breastfeeding women should be advised to use alternative methods of contraception until they discontinue breastfeeding. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for therapy and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed child from the drug or the underlying maternal condition. If possible, nursing mothers should be advised to avoid oral contraceptives and instead use other forms of contraception until they have completely weaned their child. Levonorgestrel forms conjugated metabolites, while ethinyl estradiol is metabolized in the liver by CYP3A4 into estriol and estrone. The half-life of levonorgestrel is approximately 22–49 hours after a single dose, and the half-life of ethinyl estradiol is approximately 12–23 hours. Levonorgestrel and its metabolites are excreted in urine (40–68%) and feces (16–48%), primarily as glucuronide conjugates. Ethinyl estradiol is excreted in urine and feces as glucuronide and sulfate conjugates. The above information is provided for general informational and educational purposes only.
